code.title: Divisors and primality by scanning only up to the square root
code.python:
# Divisors come in pairs (d, n/d); the smaller one is always <= sqrt(n).
# Time O(sqrt(n)), space O(number of divisors).
def divisors(n):
    small, large = [], []
    i = 1
    while i <= n // i:               # same as i*i <= n
        if n % i == 0:
            small.append(i)
            if i != n // i:          # perfect square: add the root only once
                large.append(n // i)
        i += 1
    return small + large[::-1]       # partners were found from big to small


def is_prime(n):
    if n < 2:
        return False
    i = 2
    while i <= n // i:               # any factor pair has a member <= sqrt(n)
        if n % i == 0:
            return False
        i += 1
    return True


for n in (36, 97, 91):
    d = divisors(n)
    print("n = %d divisors: %s count: %d prime: %s"
          % (n, " ".join(map(str, d)), len(d), "yes" if is_prime(n) else "no"))

followUps:
Count the square root only once: when i == n / i the two partners are the same number, so add 1 instead of 2.

Example: 36 has the pairs (1, 36), (2, 18), (3, 12), (4, 9) and then (6, 6). Four real pairs give 8 divisors and the root 6 gives 1 more, so the count is 9, not 10. This is also why only perfect squares have an odd number of divisors.

for (long i = 1; i <= n / i; i++)
  if (n % i == 0) count += (i == n / i) ? 1 : 2;

Time O(√N), space O(1).

About one million loop steps, which is fine: √(1012) = 106, and a million divisions take a few milliseconds.

It stops being fine in two cases. First, many queries: 105 numbers of that size cost 1011 steps, far too slow. Second, bigger numbers: for N = 1018 the loop needs 109 steps for a single number. In those cases switch to a sieve (small values), division by precomputed primes only, or Miller–Rabin for a yes/no primality answer. Remember to use a 64-bit type and the bound i <= n / i, because i * i on an int overflows.

Do the expensive work once, before the queries, instead of once per number.

  • Values up to about 107: build a sieve once in O(N log log N); each test is then one array lookup, O(1). A smallest-prime-factor sieve also gives the full factorisation in O(log N).
  • Values up to 1012: sieve the primes up to 106 (there are 78,498) and divide only by those, about 13 times fewer divisions than trying every number.
  • Values up to 1018: Miller–Rabin, about 12 fast powers per number.

Example: 105 queries below 106 cost about 3 × 106 steps with a sieve, against up to 108 with trial division.

code.title: Sieve for many small queries, trial division for a few big numbers
code.python:
# Trial division: best for one or a few numbers. Time O(sqrt(n)), space O(1).
def is_prime_trial(n):
    if n < 2:
        return False
    i = 2
    while i <= n // i:
        if n % i == 0:
            return False
        i += 1
    return True


# Sieve: best for many queries on small values. Time O(N log log N), space O(N).
def sieve(n):
    composite = bytearray(n + 1)
    p = 2
    while p * p <= n:
        if not composite[p]:
            for m in range(p * p, n + 1, p):   # cross out multiples
                composite[m] = 1
        p += 1
    return composite


limit = 50
composite = sieve(limit)                       # built once
primes = [str(i) for i in range(2, limit + 1) if not composite[i]]
print("sieve up to %d: %s" % (limit, " ".join(primes)))
for q in (15, 37, 49):                         # each query is now an O(1) lookup
    print("lookup %d: %s" % (q, "composite" if composite[q] else "prime"))
for n in (1000000007, 1000000001):             # too big to sieve, so divide up to sqrt(n)
    print("trial division %d: %s" % (n, "prime" if is_prime_trial(n) else "composite"))

followUps:
It depends on whether the language stores each flag in a whole byte or in one bit.

StructurePer flagN = 108
Java boolean[]1 byteabout 100 MB
C++ vector<bool>1 bitabout 12.5 MB
Python bytearray1 byteabout 100 MB

100 MB is risky under a 256 MB limit, and a Python list of booleans is far worse (8 bytes per slot, about 800 MB). To shrink it, use a bit set (java.util.BitSet, 12.5 MB), store odd numbers only (half again), or use a segmented sieve that keeps only one cache-sized block in memory.

Because Carmichael numbers are composite yet pass the Fermat check for every base that shares no factor with them, so the test calls them prime.

Fermat's test checks an−1 mod n = 1. That is always true for a prime n, but it is not a proof of primality. The smallest Carmichael number is 561 = 3 × 11 × 17, and 2560 mod 561 = 1.

Miller–Rabin fixes this by also looking at the square roots of 1 on the way. For 561 and base 2: 2140 mod 561 = 67 and 2280 mod 561 = 1. So 672 gives 1 although 67 is neither 1 nor 560. A prime modulus allows only those two square roots of 1, so 561 is composite.

code.title: Counting the sieve's cross-outs: why it is almost linear
code.python:
# Sieve of Eratosthenes that also counts how many cross-outs it performs.
# Time O(N log log N), space O(N).
def run(n):
    composite = bytearray(n + 1)
    cross_outs = 0
    p = 2
    while p * p <= n:                      # outer loop stops at sqrt(N)
        if not composite[p]:               # only primes cross out
            m = p * p                      # start at p*p: smaller multiples are done
            while m <= n:
                composite[m] = 1
                cross_outs += 1            # about N/p of these for each prime p
                m += p
        p += 1
    primes = sum(1 for i in range(2, n + 1) if not composite[i])
    # cross-outs per 100 numbers grows extremely slowly: that is the log log N factor
    print("N = %d primes = %d cross-outs = %d per 100 numbers = %d"
          % (n, primes, cross_outs, cross_outs * 100 // n))


for size in (100, 10000, 1000000):
    run(size)

followUps:
It is a sieve that crosses out every composite number exactly once, by its smallest prime factor, so the total work is O(N) instead of O(N log log N).

for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) {
  if (spf[i] == 0) { spf[i] = i; primes.add(i); }
  for (int p : primes) {
    if (p > spf[i] || (long) i * p > n) break;
    spf[i * p] = p;
  }
}

Example: 12 is marked only as 6 × 2 (smallest prime 2), never as 4 × 3, because the loop for i = 4 stops after p = 2.

It is useful when you need the spf array: factorising any number in O(log N), or computing functions such as Euler's totient or divisor counts for all numbers in O(N). For a plain prime list the ordinary sieve is just as fast in practice.

Because every multiple of p smaller than p × p was already crossed out by a smaller prime.

A multiple below p × p has the form k × p with k < p. If k ≥ 2, then k has a prime factor q that is at most k, so q < p, and the number k × p was crossed out when the sieve handled q.

Example with p = 7: 14, 28 and 42 were crossed out by 2, 21 by 3, and 35 by 5. The first number that only 7 can remove is 49 = 7 × 7.

The same argument explains why the outer loop stops at √N: once p × p > N there is nothing left to cross out. In code, compute p * p in 64 bits, since it overflows an int when p is above 46,340.

code.title: Euclid's gcd with a step counter (Fibonacci is the worst case)
code.python:
# Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b), and gcd(a, 0) = a.
# Time O(log min(a, b)), space O(1).
def show(a, b):
    x, y = a, b
    steps = 0
    while y != 0:
        r = x % y        # common divisors of (x, y) and (y, r) are the same
        x = y
        y = r
        steps += 1       # the larger number at least halves every two steps
    print("gcd(%d, %d) = %d in %d steps" % (a, b, x, steps))


show(1071, 462)
show(48, 18)
show(1000000000000, 999999999999)
# Worst case: consecutive Fibonacci numbers, every quotient is 1
show(89, 55)
show(1134903170, 701408733)

followUps:
It returns the gcd g together with two whole numbers x and y such that a × x + b × y = g.

Example: for a = 35 and b = 15 it returns g = 5, x = 1, y = −2, because 35 × 1 + 15 × (−2) = 5.

Why it is useful:

  • Modular inverse: if gcd(a, m) = 1 then a × x + m × y = 1, so x is the inverse of a modulo m. For a = 3, m = 7 we get 3 × (−2) + 7 × 1 = 1, and −2 is 5 modulo 7 (check: 3 × 5 = 15 = 2 × 7 + 1). Unlike Fermat, this works when m is not prime.
  • Equations a × x + b × y = c: solvable in whole numbers exactly when g divides c.

Cost: the same as Euclid, O(log min(a, b)) time.

For a whole array, fold the gcd from left to right; for a sliding window you need a structure that can answer range gcd queries, because gcd cannot be "undone" when an element leaves.

long g = 0;                // gcd(0, x) = x
for (long x : arr) g = gcd(g, x);

Example: [12, 18, 30] gives 12, then gcd(12, 18) = 6, then gcd(6, 30) = 6. Time O(n + log max), because g only ever shrinks; space O(1). You can stop early when g becomes 1.

Sliding window options: a sparse table (O(n log n) build, each query combines two overlapping blocks), a segment tree (O(log n) per query), or a queue made of two stacks that each keep running gcds (amortised O(1) gcd calls per step).

code.title: Arithmetic modulo 1e9+7: 64-bit products and a Fermat inverse
code.python:
M = 1_000_000_007   # prime, and just under 2^30


# The product of two residues is below about 10^18 (fits in 64 bits in other languages;
# Python integers never overflow).
def mul(a, b):
    return a * b % M


# Fast power, O(log e) time, O(1) space. (Python's built-in pow(a, e, M) does the same.)
def power(a, e):
    result = 1
    a %= M
    while e > 0:
        if e & 1:
            result = mul(result, a)
        a = mul(a, a)
        e >>= 1
    return result


a, b = 999_999_999, 999_999_998
print("a = %d b = %d M = %d" % (a, b, M))
print("(a + b) mod M =", (a + b) % M)
print("(a * b) mod M =", mul(a, b))
inv = power(a, M - 2)            # Fermat: works only because M is prime
print("inverse of a =", inv)
print("a * inverse mod M =", mul(a, inv))
print("12 / 4 done as 12 * inverse(4) =", mul(12, power(4, M - 2)))

followUps:
Division breaks: with a composite modulus some non-zero numbers have no modular inverse, so "divide by b" may be impossible.

Example with modulus 12: 4 × x mod 12 can only be 0, 4 or 8, never 1, so 4 has no inverse. Also 4 × 3 = 12 gives 0, so two non-zero values multiply to zero. An inverse of b exists only when gcd(b, m) = 1.

Fermat's shortcut bm−2 is also wrong for composite m. Addition, subtraction and multiplication still work normally.

What to do instead: avoid division (build nCr with Pascal's triangle, O(n2)), use extended Euclid when the gcd happens to be 1, or solve modulo each prime power and join the results with the Chinese Remainder Theorem.

You need a 128-bit intermediate result, because the product of two numbers near 1018 is near 1036 and a 64-bit type holds only about 9.2 × 1018.

  • C++: (__int128) a * b % m.
  • Java: BigInteger, or Math.multiplyHigh for the top 64 bits.
  • Python: a * b % m just works.
  • Anywhere: multiply by doubling, which only ever adds numbers below m:
long r = 0; a %= m;
while (b > 0) {
  if ((b & 1) == 1) r = (r + a) % m;
  a = (a + a) % m; b >>= 1;
}

Doubling costs O(log b), about 60 additions, instead of O(1), and is safe for m up to about 4.6 × 1018.

code.title: Safe modular add, subtract and multiply helpers
code.python:
M = 1_000_000_007


# Each helper returns a value in [0, M). Time O(1), space O(1).
def add(a, b):
    return (a % M + b % M) % M


# Python's % is already non-negative for a positive M; the "+ M" form is kept
# so the same line is also correct in Java, C++ and JavaScript.
def sub(a, b):
    return ((a - b) % M + M) % M


# Python integers never overflow; other languages need 64 bits here.
def mul(a, b):
    return (a % M) * (b % M) % M


a, b, c = 1_000_000_006, 1_000_000_005, 123_456_789
print("a = %d b = %d c = %d M = %d" % (a, b, c, M))
print("add(a, b) =", add(a, b))
print("sub(b, a) =", sub(b, a))        # the raw value is -1
print("sub(3, 5) =", sub(3, 5))        # the raw value is -2
print("mul(a, b) =", mul(a, b))
# Three factors: reduce after every multiplication
print("mul(mul(a, b), c) =", mul(mul(a, b), c))
real1, real2 = M + 1, 5                # the real values: real1 is the larger one
print("real values %d > %d but residues are %d and %d (never compare residues)"
      % (real1, real2, real1 % M, real2 % M))

followUps:
Because a remainder tells you nothing about which real number was bigger, so the maximum of two remainders can pick the smaller real value.

Example with M = 109 + 7: the real values 1,000,000,008 and 5 have remainders 1 and 5. Math.max(1, 5) picks 5, but the first value was really the larger one, and the final answer is wrong.

The rule: taking the remainder is safe only for sums and products (counting problems). For max or min problems, keep the true values: usually they fit in a long, and if they can be huge, compare with something that keeps order (for example logarithms, or exact big integers) and store the remainder only alongside it for printing.

Math.floorMod(a, m) gives a result with the sign of the divisor m, so for a positive m it is never negative; % gives a result with the sign of the left side a.

ExpressionResult
-7 % 3−1
Math.floorMod(-7, 3)2
7 % 3 and floorMod(7, 3)1

So floorMod(a - b, M) replaces ((a - b) % M + M) % M, and it behaves like Python's %. The two differ only when the signs of a and m differ. It does not protect against overflow: a - b or a * b must still fit in the type before the call.

code.title: Binary exponentiation with its edge cases
code.python:
# Binary exponentiation: a^b mod m. Time O(log b), space O(1).
# (Python's built-in pow(a, b, m) does the same job.)
def mod_pow(a, b, m):
    result = 1 % m            # 1 % m gives 0 when m = 1
    base = a % m              # reduce first; Python's % also fixes a negative a
    while b > 0:
        if b & 1:             # this bit of b is set
            result = result * base % m
        base = base * base % m    # square for the next bit
        b >>= 1               # drop the bit just used
    return result


def show(a, b, m):
    print("%d^%d mod %d = %d" % (a, b, m, mod_pow(a, b, m)))


show(2, 10, 1000)
show(3, 10**18, 1000000007)      # only about 60 rounds
show(5, 0, 1)                    # edge: m = 1
show(-2, 3, 7)                   # edge: negative base
show(0, 5, 13)                   # edge: a = 0
show(1000000008, 2, 1000000007)  # edge: a >= m

followUps:
Because it computes the same half twice, and each of those computes its half twice, so the number of calls doubles at every level and the total becomes O(b) instead of O(log b).

The cost follows T(b) = 2 × T(b/2) + 1, which adds up to about b calls. For b = 16 that is 31 calls instead of 5. For b = 1018 it never finishes, while the correct version needs about 60 steps.

The fix is to compute the half once and reuse it:

long half = pow(a, b / 2, m);
long res = half * half % m;
if (b % 2 == 1) res = res * (a % m) % m;
return res;

Space is O(log b) for the recursion; the loop version uses O(1).

Replace the number a by a 2 × 2 matrix and use the same square-and-multiply loop: raising the matrix [[1, 1], [1, 0]] to the power n gives [[F(n+1), F(n)], [F(n), F(n−1)]].

One multiplication by that matrix turns the pair (F(n), F(n−1)) into (F(n+1), F(n)), so n steps are the n-th power, and a power needs only about log2 n squarings.

Example: the matrix squared is [[2, 1], [1, 1]], which reads F(3) = 2, F(2) = 1, F(1) = 1. Squaring again gives [[5, 3], [3, 2]]: F(5) = 5, F(4) = 3.

Cost: O(log n) matrix multiplications of 8 number multiplications each, O(1) space. For n = 1018 that is about 60 squarings, with every entry reduced modulo M.

code.title: nCr mod p with factorial and inverse-factorial tables
code.python:
P = 1_000_000_007
N = 1000

# Precompute once: O(N + log P) time, O(N) space. Each query is then O(1).
fact = [1] * (N + 1)
for i in range(1, N + 1):
    fact[i] = fact[i - 1] * i % P

inv_fact = [1] * (N + 1)
inv_fact[N] = pow(fact[N], P - 2, P)          # one Fermat inverse only
for i in range(N, 0, -1):
    inv_fact[i - 1] = inv_fact[i] * i % P     # fill downward


def ncr(n, r):
    if r < 0 or r > n:                        # guard: impossible choices
        return 0
    return fact[n] * inv_fact[r] % P * inv_fact[n - r] % P   # reduce after each multiply


for n, r in ((5, 2), (10, 3), (52, 5), (1000, 500), (3, 5)):
    print("C(%d, %d) mod P = %d" % (n, r, ncr(n, r)))

followUps:
Because i! = i × (i−1)!, so dividing both sides out gives 1/(i−1)! = (1/i!) × i. Multiplying the inverse of i! by i cancels the extra factor i and leaves the inverse of (i−1)!.

Example modulo 7: 3! = 6 and its inverse is 6 (6 × 6 = 36 = 5 × 7 + 1). Then invFact[2] = 6 × 3 = 18, which is 4 modulo 7. Check: 2! × 4 = 8, which is 1 modulo 7. Correct.

Why go backward: it needs only one modular power (for invFact[N]) and then one multiplication per entry, O(N + log p) in total. Computing every inverse with its own power would cost O(N log p), about 30 times more for p = 109 + 7.

Count all paths with one binomial coefficient, then subtract the paths that touch a blocked cell, counting each bad path once at the first blocked cell it hits.

  1. Paths from (0, 0) to (r, c) moving right or down: C(r + c, r).
  2. Sort the blocked cells by row, then column, and add the target as the last cell.
  3. For each cell i: dp[i] = paths(start → i) − Σ dp[j] × paths(j → i) over earlier cells j that lie above and to the left of i.
dp[i] = ways(0, 0, x[i], y[i]);
for (j < i) if (x[j] <= x[i] && y[j] <= y[i])
  dp[i] -= dp[j] * ways(x[j], y[j], x[i], y[i]);

Example: to (2, 2) there are C(4, 2) = 6 paths; blocking (1, 1) removes 2 × 2 = 4, leaving 2. Cost O(k2) for k blocked cells after the O(N) factorial tables.

code.title: Pigeonhole: a subarray whose sum is divisible by n
code.python:
# Pigeonhole: n + 1 prefix sums but only n remainders, so two prefixes share one.
# The elements between those two prefixes add up to a multiple of n.
# Time O(n), space O(n).
a = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5]
n = len(a)
first = [-1] * n          # first[r] = prefix length where remainder r appeared
first[0] = 0              # the empty prefix has sum 0
print("array:", " ".join(map(str, a)))
total = 0
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    total += a[i - 1]
    r = total % n         # Python's % is already non-negative
    if first[r] != -1:    # repeat found: guaranteed by pigeonhole
        start, end = first[r], i - 1
        part = a[start:end + 1]
        print("remainder %d seen after %d and after %d elements" % (r, start, i))
        print("subarray [%d..%d]: %s sum = %d divisible by %d"
              % (start, end, " ".join(map(str, part)), sum(part), n))
        break
    first[r] = i

followUps:
Anywhere you repeatedly apply the same rule to a value that can take only a limited number of states: after more steps than there are states, some state must repeat, and from then on the sequence loops.

  • Decimal expansion of 1/7: the remainders in long division are below 7, so a remainder repeats within 6 steps and the digits 142857 repeat forever.
  • Happy numbers: the sum of squared digits of a number below 1000 is at most 243, so the chain must loop.
  • Random number generators of the form x → (a × x + c) mod m repeat within m steps.
  • Powers ak mod m and Fibonacci numbers modulo m are periodic.

Once a cycle is guaranteed, find it with a hash set (O(states) memory) or Floyd's two pointers (O(1) memory).

Pigeonhole is a guarantee, the birthday paradox is a probability: pigeonhole says a collision is certain once you have more items than boxes, while the birthday paradox says a collision becomes likely much earlier, at roughly the square root of the number of boxes.

Example with 365 possible birthdays: you need 366 people to be sure two share a birthday, but only 23 people for a chance above 50%.

In algorithms: pigeonhole gives proofs and worst-case bounds (a duplicate must exist among n + 1 values in [1, n]). The birthday effect gives expected behaviour: a 32-bit hash typically sees its first collision after about 77,000 keys, not 4 billion, and Pollard's rho finds a factor p in about √p steps.

code.title: Find the duplicate with Floyd's cycle detection
code.python:
# Floyd's tortoise and hare on the "linked list" i -> nums[i].
# Time O(n), space O(1), and the array is never modified.
def find_duplicate(nums):
    slow, fast = nums[0], nums[nums[0]]
    while slow != fast:            # phase 1: meet somewhere inside the cycle
        slow = nums[slow]          # one step
        fast = nums[nums[fast]]    # two steps
    slow = 0                       # phase 2: restart one pointer from index 0
    while slow != fast:            # same speed: they meet at the cycle entry
        slow = nums[slow]
        fast = nums[fast]
    return slow                    # the cycle entry is the duplicate value


def show(nums):
    print("array: %s -> duplicate: %d" % (" ".join(map(str, nums)), find_duplicate(nums)))


show([1, 3, 4, 2, 2])
show([3, 1, 3, 4, 2])
show([2, 2, 2, 2, 2])
show([1, 1])

followUps:
The distance from the start to the cycle entry equals, modulo the cycle length, the distance from the meeting point forward to the entry, so two pointers walking at the same speed from those two places arrive at the entry together.

Let a = steps from the start to the entry, b = steps from the entry to the meeting point, L = cycle length. When they meet, slow has walked a + b and fast 2(a + b). Fast is ahead by whole laps, so a + b = k × L, which means a = k × L − b.

Now walk a steps from the meeting point: the position inside the cycle is b + a = k × L, exactly the entry. The pointer from the start also needs a steps to reach the entry.

Example [1, 3, 4, 2, 2]: the walk is 0 → 1 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 2, so a = 3 and L = 2. They meet at index 4 (b = 1), and a + b = 4 = 2 × L.

Because both break a rule of the problem: sorting changes the array (or needs a copy), and a hash set needs extra memory that grows with n.

  • Sort in place: O(n log n) time, but the array is read-only.
  • Sort a copy or use a hash set / boolean array: O(n) extra space, but only O(1) is allowed.
  • Marking visited values by flipping signs: O(1) space, but it also writes into the array.

Two methods respect both rules. Floyd's cycle detection: O(n) time. Binary search on the value: count how many numbers are ≤ mid; if the count is more than mid, the duplicate is ≤ mid. For [1, 3, 4, 2, 2], three numbers are ≤ 2, and 3 > 2, so the duplicate is 1 or 2. That costs O(n log n) time and O(1) space.

code.title: Divisor counts for 1..N by walking multiples
code.python:
# For every d, add 1 to each multiple of d. Work = N/1 + N/2 + ... + N/N, about N ln N.
# Time O(N log N), space O(N).
def divisor_counts(n):
    count = [0] * (n + 1)
    work = 0
    for d in range(1, n + 1):
        for m in range(d, n + 1, d):   # d divides m, 2d, 3d, ...
            count[m] += 1
            work += 1
    return count, work


small, work = divisor_counts(12)
print("divisor counts for 1..12:", " ".join(map(str, small[1:])))
print("inner loop steps for N = 12:", work)

n = 100000
big, work = divisor_counts(n)
best = 1
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    if big[i] > big[best]:             # first number with the most divisors
        best = i
print("inner loop steps for N = %d: %d" % (n, work))
print("most divisors up to %d: %d has %d" % (n, best, big[best]))

followUps:
1344 divisors, reached by 735,134,400.

The divisor count comes from the prime factorisation: multiply (exponent + 1) over all primes. 735,134,400 = 26 × 33 × 52 × 7 × 11 × 13 × 17, so the count is 7 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 1344. Numbers with many divisors always look like this: small primes, with exponents that do not increase.

Useful figures to remember: at most 240 divisors up to 106, 1344 up to 109, and 103,680 up to 1018. The practical meaning: a loop over the divisors of one number is tiny compared with the number itself, roughly the cube root of N in the worst case, so "for each divisor" inside another loop is usually affordable.

Use a sieve: start with phi[i] = i, and for every prime p remove the fraction 1/p from all multiples of p.

  1. Fill phi[i] = i for all i.
  2. Go through i = 2..N. If phi[i] is still i, then i is prime.
  3. For each multiple m of that prime, do phi[m] −= phi[m] / p.
for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) phi[i] = i;
for (int p = 2; p <= n; p++)
  if (phi[p] == p)                      // p is prime
    for (int m = p; m <= n; m += p)
      phi[m] -= phi[m] / p;

Example for 12: start at 12; prime 2 gives 12 − 6 = 6; prime 3 gives 6 − 2 = 4. Indeed 1, 5, 7 and 11 are the four numbers coprime to 12. Time O(N log log N), space O(N).

code.title: Counting pairs whose product is divisible by k using gcds
code.python:
from math import gcd


# k divides x*y exactly when k divides gcd(x,k) * gcd(y,k).
# Time O(N * d(k) + N log k), space O(k); d(k) = number of divisors of k.
def count_pairs(nums, k):
    divs = [d for d in range(1, k + 1) if k % d == 0]   # all possible gcd values
    seen = [0] * (k + 1)       # seen[g] = earlier elements whose gcd with k is g
    pairs = 0
    for x in nums:
        g = gcd(x, k)          # only this part of x matters
        for d in divs:
            if g * d % k == 0:  # partner groups that work
                pairs += seen[d]
        seen[g] += 1
    return pairs


def show(nums, k):
    print("nums: %s k = %d -> pairs = %d" % (" ".join(map(str, nums)), k, count_pairs(nums, k)))


show([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 2)
show([1, 2, 3, 4], 5)
show([6, 10, 15, 4, 9, 25], 30)

followUps:
At most 128 divisors; the number 83,160 reaches that maximum.

83,160 = 23 × 33 × 5 × 7 × 11, and the divisor count is the product of (exponent + 1): 4 × 4 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 128.

This is what makes the pair-counting solution fast. Every value is replaced by gcd(x, k), which is a divisor of k, so the map holds at most 128 different keys. For 105 elements the inner loop runs at most 105 × 128 = 1.28 × 107 times, against about 5 × 109 pairs for the brute force.

Keep two tables instead of one: how many single elements have each gcd, and how many pairs have each "combined gcd", then match each new element against the pair table.

  1. For each element compute g = gcd(x, k).
  2. Add to the answer pairCnt[d] for every divisor d with d × g divisible by k.
  3. For every divisor d with oneCnt[d] > 0, add oneCnt[d] to pairCnt[gcd(d × g, k)].
  4. Then do oneCnt[g]++.
for (d : divs) if (d * g % k == 0) ans += pairCnt[d];
for (d : divs) pairCnt[gcd(d * g, k)] += oneCnt[d];
oneCnt[g]++;

The order matters, so an element is never combined with itself. Example: [2, 3, 5], k = 30: after 2 and 3 the pair table has pairCnt[6] = 1; for 5, 6 × 5 = 30 is divisible by 30, so the answer is 1. Time O(N × d(k) × log k), space O(d(k)).

The idea still works, but two things must change: the product g × g' no longer fits in 64 bits, and k can have up to 6720 divisors, so looping over all divisors for every element is too slow.

  • Overflow: since g divides k, test "(k / g) divides g'" instead of "k divides g × g'". Example: k = 12, g = 4, g' = 6: k / g = 3 and 3 divides 6, so 4 × 6 = 24 is divisible by 12.
  • Speed: first count how many elements have each gcd (a hash map with long keys). Then, for each divisor d, compute mult[d] = number of elements whose gcd is a multiple of d. The answer is the sum over distinct g of cnt[g] × mult[k / g], minus the elements paired with themselves, divided by 2.

Cost: O(N log k) for the gcds plus at most d(k)2 ≈ 4.5 × 107 simple steps.

code.title: Multiplying modulo a number near 1e18 without overflow
code.python:
# "Multiply by doubling": a * b mod m using only additions that stay below 2m.
# Python does not need it (integers never overflow) but the idea is the same everywhere.
# Time O(log b), space O(1).
def mul_mod(a, b, m):
    result = 0
    a %= m
    while b > 0:
        if b & 1:                     # add a when this bit of b is set
            result = (result + a) % m
        a = (a + a) % m               # double a for the next bit
        b >>= 1
    return result


def show(a, b, m):
    got = mul_mod(a, b, m)
    assert got == a * b % m           # cross-check with Python's big integers
    print("%d * %d mod %d = %d" % (a, b, m, got))


show(7, 8, 10)
show(987654321987654321, 123456789123456789, 1000000000000000003)
show(999999999999999999, 999999999999999999, 1000000000000000000)

followUps:
Montgomery reduction is a way to compute a × b mod m without any division: it replaces the slow "% m" by two multiplications and a shift.

Numbers are stored in a shifted form, a × R mod m, where R = 264. After multiplying two such numbers, the REDC step adds a carefully chosen multiple of m so that the low 64 bits become zero, and then drops those bits, which is a division by R done as a free shift. One final subtraction of m may be needed.

It is fast because a 64-bit hardware multiply takes about 3 CPU cycles, while a 128-by-64-bit division takes 30 or more. The price: m must be odd, and converting into and out of the shifted form costs extra, so it pays off only when many multiplications share one modulus, as in fast power, Miller–Rabin and Pollard's rho.

It uses fast power to compute one starting value ad mod n, and then just squares it a few times while looking for the value n − 1.

  1. Write n − 1 = d × 2s with d odd.
  2. For a base a, compute x = ad mod n with binary exponentiation.
  3. If x is 1 or n − 1, this base passes.
  4. Otherwise square x up to s − 1 times; if it becomes n − 1, the base passes. If it never does, n is composite.

Example n = 221: 220 = 55 × 22. Base 137: 13755 mod 221 = 188, squared gives 205; neither is 220, so 221 is composite (13 × 17).

Each base costs O(log n) modular multiplications, and for n near 1018 each of them needs a 128-bit-safe multiply. The 12 bases 2..37 give a guaranteed answer for all 64-bit numbers.

code.title: Stress test: fast nCr against a Pascal-triangle brute force
code.python:
P = 1_000_000_007
N = 60

fact = [1] * (N + 1)
for i in range(1, N + 1):
    fact[i] = fact[i - 1] * i % P
inv_fact = [1] * (N + 1)
inv_fact[N] = pow(fact[N], P - 2, P)
for i in range(N, 0, -1):
    inv_fact[i - 1] = inv_fact[i] * i % P


# The fast version under test: factorials and inverse factorials.
def fast(n, r):
    if r < 0 or r > n:
        return 0
    return fact[n] * inv_fact[r] % P * inv_fact[n - r] % P


# Stress test: compare with a slow but obviously correct Pascal triangle.
# Time O(N^2), space O(N^2).
pascal = [[0] * (N + 2) for _ in range(N + 1)]   # brute force: C(n,r) = C(n-1,r-1) + C(n-1,r)
for n in range(N + 1):
    pascal[n][0] = 1
    for r in range(1, n + 1):
        pascal[n][r] = (pascal[n - 1][r - 1] + pascal[n - 1][r]) % P

checked = mismatches = 0
for n in range(N + 1):
    for r in range(n + 2):                       # r = n + 1 tests the "return 0" guard
        checked += 1
        if fast(n, r) != pascal[n][r]:
            mismatches += 1
print("checked %d (n, r) pairs up to n = %d, mismatches: %d" % (checked, N, mismatches))
print("C(60, 30) mod P: fast = %d brute = %d" % (fast(60, 30), pascal[60][30]))

followUps:
A very common one is multiplying three residues in one expression, which overflows even a 64-bit type.

// looks fine, is wrong
return fact[n] * invFact[r] * invFact[n - r] % MOD;
// correct: reduce after each multiplication
return fact[n] * invFact[r] % MOD * invFact[n - r] % MOD;

Each factor is below 109 + 7, so two of them give about 1018 (fits in a long), but three give about 1027, far above 9.2 × 1018. The bug is subtle because small tests pass: C(5, 2) uses tiny factorials. Only when the inverse factorials look like random 9-digit numbers does the result silently wrap around.

Other frequent ones: (a - b) % MOD going negative, and (int) a * b multiplying in 32 bits before widening.

Compare the fast function against a slow version that is obviously correct, on every small input and on many random ones, and print the first input where they differ.

  1. Oracle: Pascal's triangle modulo p for n ≤ 60 or so (only additions, nothing to get wrong), or Python's math.comb(n, r) % p for big n.
  2. Exhaustive small cases: every n from 0 to 60 and every r from −1 to n + 1. This covers r = 0, r = n, n = 0 and the "return 0" guards.
  3. Large cases: random n up to the table limit, plus the limit itself, to catch overflow and off-by-one array sizes.
  4. Identities when no oracle is available: C(n, r) = C(n, n − r), and C(n, r) = C(n−1, r−1) + C(n−1, r) modulo p.

Example check: C(5, 2) must be 10 and C(3, 5) must be 0. The exhaustive part is only about 2000 comparisons, so it runs instantly.
